Figure 4.1. Median p95 latency (ms) by platform and scenario. Row order places the four traditional configurations before the three managed container-based platforms. This figure visualises the median p95 values recorded in Table 4.2.

Figure 4.2. Median p99 latency by platform and scenario; asterisks inside cells flag one or more timeout-censored replications, so the displayed p99 is a lower-bound indicator. This figure visualises the median p99 values recorded in Table 4.2.

Figure 4.3. Balanced descriptive p95 contrast by scenario. Paired bars show the median of platform-level cell medians within the traditional and managed groups; the values are the balanced descriptive summaries reported in Table 4.10.
Figure 4.4. Median callback-defined goodput by platform and scenario. This figure visualises the goodput values recorded in Table 4.3.

Figure 4.5. Median callback-defined request-failure rate by platform and scenario. Scenario-wise horizontal bars show the median percentage request-failure rate recorded in Table 4.3, using a shared x-axis for direct comparison.
Figure 4.6. Median Apdex by platform and scenario using the study’s Apdex parameters (T = 500 ms; F = 2,000 ms). This figure visualises the Apdex values recorded in Table 4.3.

Figure 4.7. Balanced descriptive callback-defined goodput contrast by scenario. Paired bars show the balanced group medians from Table 4.10, making the small traditional-versus-managed delivery differences directly readable.

Figure 4.8. Warm-up ratio by platform across steady scenarios A–C, separated into traditional and managed platform families. Reference line = 1.0; values below 1.0 indicate lower early p95 than later p95, and values above 1.0 indicate higher early p95. This figure visualises the warm-up evidence recorded in Table 4.5.

Figure 4.9. Scenario D burst phase-level p95 summary (log scale). Each line connects the exact phase-level p95 summaries from Table 4.6: baseline p95, peak-window p95, peak-maximum p95, and post-ramp p95. Labels identify peak-window cells where the retained per-second p95 exceeded one second.

Figure 4.10. Supplementary post-idle first-request latency versus immediate warm repeat for managed platforms. Grouped median bars compare the first request after the script-defined 360-second no-probe interval with the immediate warm repeat (log-scale x-axis). Multiplier labels use the median of the valid within-pair first/repeat ratios, matching Table 4.7. Koyeb has four valid pairs out of five attempted. This descriptive probe is outside the 280-run primary matrix.
Figure 4.11. Replication-level p95 latency medians with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals by scenario.

Figure 4.12. Modelled warm cost against median p95 latency. Each marker is one platform-scenario cell: the horizontal position is the platform’s modelled USD per million callback-qualified responses (Table 4.12; log scale) and the vertical position is the cell-median p95 latency (Table 4.2; log scale); marker shape encodes the scenario. The plot is conditional decision-support evidence under the stated warm-cost assumptions, not an overall ranking.
